title: Oncological surgical emergencies
subtitle: Neutropenic enterocolitis, tumour perforation, tumour bleeding

sources.org: National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE)
sources.title: Neutropenic sepsis: prevention and management in people with cancer (CG151)
Management of febrile neutropaenia: ESMO Clinical Practice Guidelines (Klastersky J et al., Ann Oncol)
Neutropenic enterocolitis, a growing concern in the era of widespread use of aggressive chemotherapy (Nesher L, Rolston KV)
2017 WSES guidelines on colon and rectal cancer emergencies: obstruction and perforation (Pisano M et al., World J Emerg Surg)
Guidelines for the use of platelet transfusions (Estcourt LJ et al., Br J Haematol)

red_flags.text: Fever and abdominal pain, often right iliac fossa, within weeks of chemotherapy: neutropenic enterocolitis until proven otherwise.
Peritonism, free gas or a rising lactate in a neutropenic patient: perforation. Neutropenia blunts the signs, so a soft-looking abdomen does not reassure.
Haematemesis, melaena or rectal bleeding from a known tumour with tachycardia or a falling haemoglobin.
Thrombocytopenia or coagulopathy from chemotherapy or marrow infiltration in any bleeding patient.
Steroid therapy masking peritonitis and fever.

do_now.text: Suspected neutropenic sepsis: treat as an emergency and give empiric broad-spectrum IV antibiotics immediately, without waiting for the neutrophil count.
Neutropenic enterocolitis: choose an empiric regimen that also covers anaerobes, per local febrile neutropenia protocol.
Sepsis resuscitation: IV access, cultures, lactate, fluids, and early critical care review for hypotension.
Bleeding tumour: two large-bore cannulae, crossmatch, major haemorrhage protocol if shocked, and stop or reverse anticoagulants.

assess.text: Neutrophil count and its expected trajectory: the date of the last chemotherapy and whether count recovery is days or weeks away.
Risk-stratify febrile neutropenia; a surgical abdomen is never low risk whatever the score.
Severity of sepsis and organ dysfunction.
Cancer status and prognosis: curative or palliative intent, and what the oncologist plans next. This shapes the extent of any operation.
Bleeding source: luminal tumour (stomach, colon), intraperitoneal tumour rupture (liver), or a fistula into a vessel.

investigate.text: Blood cultures before antibiotics where this causes no delay, FBC with differential, coagulation, U&E, LFT, lactate, crossmatch.
CT abdomen and pelvis with IV contrast: bowel wall thickening (typically caecal), pneumatosis, free gas, collection, or an active blush.
CT angiography for active bleeding to localise the source for radiology or endoscopy.
Stool testing for Clostridioides difficile in any neutropenic patient with diarrhoea.

resuscitate.text: Neutropenic enterocolitis without perforation: bowel rest, IV fluids, nasogastric decompression if distended, and antibiotics. Most settle without an operation.
Consider granulocyte colony-stimulating factor with the oncologist for a patient with febrile neutropenia and a severe infection.
Correct thrombocytopenia and coagulopathy before and during an operation; a platelet count of at least 50 x 10^9/L is the usual threshold for major surgery.
Transfuse to restrictive targets unless bleeding is massive, using blood components early in haemorrhage.

definitive.text: Operate on neutropenic enterocolitis for free perforation, persistent bleeding after correction of coagulopathy and thrombocytopenia, or deterioration despite full medical treatment. Resect all necrotic bowel and favour a stoma over an anastomosis.
Perforation at a colonic tumour: resection with oncological principles where possible; with diastatic caecal perforation proximal to an obstructing tumour, a subtotal colectomy.
In a septic, unstable patient, damage control: resect, control contamination, leave in discontinuity or form a stoma, and return.

Bleeding tumour: endoscopic haemostasis for luminal lesions, angiographic embolisation where available, and surgery when these fail or are unavailable. Palliative radiotherapy controls slower tumour bleeding.

escalate.text: Consultant surgeon, oncologist or haematologist, and critical care together. Neutropenic patients deteriorate faster than the observations suggest.
Interventional radiology early for a bleeding tumour or a drainable collection.
Palliative care where the cancer is advanced and the operation would not change the outcome that matters to the patient.

notes: The neutropenic abdomen lies: no pus, little guarding, and a near-normal white count. CT findings and the trend in the patient carry the diagnosis.
Neutropenic enterocolitis is mainly a medical disease with a few clearly defined surgical indications. Knowing those indications is the surgical skill.
An emergency cancer operation is still a cancer operation. Where the patient is stable enough, a proper oncological resection now avoids a second operation later.
